viral_tweets.title_en:
F*ck yes. I got GTA 6 running on PC before Rockstar did.

Rockstar only released it on PS5 and Xbox, and PC players were told to wait. I didn't wait. I handed the whole setup to Claude Code and watched it boot the game in five seconds.

I typed one line: "boot GTA 6 on this PC and start story mode."

First it checked whether my machine could even handle it: GPU, CPU, RAM, Vulkan. Then it verified the game files and mounted every archive, the same way the game does it on a console. The slowest part on any new setup is the shader cache, so it compiled all 18,432 shaders up front instead of letting the game stutter through them later. After that it signed in, set 1440p, picked story mode and launched it.

Five seconds of terminal, then the Rockstar logo.

I've been playing for three hours. Haven't seen a single stutter.

My friend called to brag about his new PS5 Pro. I sent him this video. He still hasn't replied.

The prompt I used is in the replies.

viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_en:
Remarks from Anthropic CEO @DarioAmodei on our initial public offering:

My co-founders and I started Anthropic because we believe that the most powerful technology of our time should be built for the benefit of humankind.

Daniela and I lost our father to a disease that, just a few years later, became curable. I started my career in biology, hoping to help future cures come sooner. In the lab, I saw the vast thicket of complexity that scientists face when they’re trying to understand disease and develop new treatments.

So many of the scientific tools that can cut through that thicket—tools for gene editing, gene synthesis, controlling brain cells with light—started as pure ideas. In other words, they came from thinking. From intelligence.

Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world. But progress on other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families. Going from a great idea to a treatment can take decades: it took many years from the first discovery of a strange repeating pattern in DNA to the approval of the first treatment for a disease using CRISPR.

Nature is full of these patterns. But we’ve had too little intelligence to decipher most of them; too few scientists, with too little time. Now we can build that intelligence. Whether it’s protein folding, drug design, cancer genetics, or clinical trial administration, scientists across many areas of biology and medicine are finding Claude can help them do their research in a fraction of the time it would’ve taken just a couple of years ago. I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.

I don’t want to get ahead of myself. At this point all we have are early results. Experiments and clinical trials will still take time. And although they involve slow and ponderous processes, I believe those processes can be substantially accelerated by AI. We hope that in the future fewer families miss a cure by just a few years.

Medicine is just a particularly vivid example, but there are many others. Our customers—the world’s most ambitious companies, nonprofits, and individual people—are already applying the intelligence we’ve built to stimulate economic growth; lift people out of poverty; protect democracy and free societies; even make everyday services like the DMV work better. We’re proud to work alongside them. And I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future.

At the same time, we have always been honest that this technology has very real risks. These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or nation-states, to economic disruption, to losing control of AI systems. We discuss these risks not because we think they are inevitable, but because we think they are avoidable.

Avoiding them depends on the choices made by the people building AI. There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety, versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety. And an obsession with safety and with public benefit has been woven into Anthropic’s DNA from the start. From safeguards against biological and cyber risks, to alignment training and testing, to looking inside our models like an X-ray, Anthropic has pioneered methods for understanding and steering the behavior of AI systems.

There is much work still to be done, and the most difficult safety work lies ahead of us. The incredible talent of the company that has enabled us to build the most capable AI systems will need to be directed, even more so than it has already, towards double- and triple-checking that those AI systems are safe and secure.

And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control. We will not bend to either business or political pressure. Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing.

If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top. When the race to the top is working properly, it doesn’t matter which company has the best models—everyone wins because everyone is building safely. The race to the top works best when driven from the front of the pack, and we fully hope and expect to do so, but the goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time.

The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better.

This moment is bigger than any one company, or any one country. It will take all of us, working together, to ensure this technology goes well for us and the many generations to come. Starting today, we hope that you’ll join us on this mission.
viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_zh:
Anthropic 首席执行官 @DarioAmodei 关于我们首次公开募股的评论：

我和我的联合创始人创立了 Anthropic，因为我们相信我们这个时代最强大的技术应该是为了造福人类而构建的。

丹妮拉和我的父亲因一种疾病去世，仅仅几年后，这种疾病就可以治愈。我的职业生涯始于生物学，希望能帮助未来的治愈方法早日到来。在实验室里，我看到了科学家在试图了解疾病和开发新疗法时所面临的巨大复杂性。

许多能够突破这一困境的科学工具——基因编辑、基因合成、用光控制脑细胞的工具——都是从纯粹的想法开始的。换句话说，它们来自于思考。来自智力。

人类智慧已经让世界上大部分地区的鼠疫、天花和脊髓灰质炎等疾病成为历史。但对于如此多的患者及其家人来说，其他疾病的进展太慢了。从一个伟大的想法到一种治疗方法可能需要数十年的时间：从首次发现 DNA 中奇怪的重复模式到第一个使用 CRISPR 治疗疾病的方法获得批准，花了很多年的时间。

大自然充满了这些模式。但我们的智慧太少，无法破译其中的大部分。科学家太少，时间太少。现在我们可以构建这种智能。无论是蛋白质折叠、药物设计、癌症遗传学还是临床试验管理，生物学和医学许多领域的科学家都发现克劳德可以帮助他们完成研究，所需时间只是几年前的一小部分。我相信足够强大的人工智能，与人类协同工作，可以将一个世纪的科学和医学进步压缩为十年。

我不想超越自己。目前我们所拥有的只是早期结果。实验和临床试验仍需要时间。尽管它们涉及缓慢而繁重的过程，但我相信人工智能可以大大加速这些过程。我们希望未来能有更少的家庭因仅仅几年的时间而错过治疗。

医学只是一个特别生动的例子，但还有很多其他例子。我们的客户——世界上最雄心勃勃的公司、非营利组织和个人——已经在应用我们构建的智能来刺激经济增长；让人们摆脱贫困；保护民主和自由社会；甚至让 DMV 等日常服务更好地运作。我们很自豪能与他们一起工作。我对我们未来可以一起做的事情非常乐观。

与此同时，我们一直诚实地认为这项技术存在非常现实的风险。这些问题包括个人或民族国家滥用技术、经济混乱、失去对人工智能系统的控制等。我们讨论这些风险不是因为我们认为它们是不可避免的，而是因为我们认为它们是可以避免的。

避免它们取决于构建人工智能的人们做出的选择。如果我们不关心安全，人工智能将会如何发展，而如果我们痴迷于安全，人工智能将会如何发展，两者之间存在着巨大的差异。对安全和公共利益的痴迷从一开始就融入了 Anthropic 的基因中。从防范生物和网络风险，到校准训练和测试，再到像 X 射线一样观察我们的模型，Anthropic 开创了理解和引导人工智能系统行为的方法。

任重而道远，最艰巨的安全工作还在后面。该公司拥有令人难以置信的人才，使我们能够构建最强大的人工智能系统，我们需要对其进行双重和三重检查，以确保这些人工智能系统的安全性，甚至比现在更加努力。

明确地说，我们将加快人工智能系统的训练和部署步伐，只要有必要，我们就确信它们是安全的，并将继续处于人类控制之下。我们不会屈服于商业或政治压力。今天，公司的财务状况变得更加强大，这样做只会增强我们做正确事情的决心。

如果我们能够证明我们可以在安全方面做出正确的选择，同时仍能打造一家极其成功的公司，那么我们行业的其他人也会受到启发，采取同样的做法。我们称之为登顶竞赛。当竞争顺利进行时，哪家公司拥有最好的模型并不重要——每个人都会赢，因为每个人都在安全地建造。当处于领先地位时，通往顶峰的竞争效果最好，我们完全希望并期望这样做，但目标是让整个行业变得更好，无论 Anthropic 在任何特定时间是赢还是输。

机器智能的出现是人类历史上的开创性时刻之一，我们有一个难得的机会来让它变得更好。

这一刻比任何一家公司或任何一个国家都重要。我们所有人都需要共同努力，才能确保这项技术为我们和子孙后代带来良好的发展。从今天开始，我们希望您能加入我们的行列。

大自然充满了这些模式。但我们的智慧太少，无法破译其中的大部分。科学家太少，时间太少。现在我们可以构建这种智能。无论是蛋白质折叠、药物设计、癌症遗传学还是临床试验管理，生物学和医学许多领域的科学家都发现克劳德可以帮助他们完成研究，所需时间只是几年前的一小部分。我相信足够强大的人工智能，与人类协同工作，可以将一个世纪的科学和医学进步压缩为十年。

我不想超越自己。目前我们所拥有的只是早期结果。实验和临床试验仍需要时间。尽管它们涉及缓慢而繁重的过程，但我相信人工智能可以大大加速这些过程。我们希望未来能有更少的家庭因仅仅几年的时间而错过治疗。

医学只是一个特别生动的例子，但还有很多其他例子。我们的客户——世界上最雄心勃勃的公司、非营利组织和个人——已经在应用我们构建的智能来刺激经济增长；让人们摆脱贫困；保护民主和自由社会；甚至让 DMV 等日常服务更好地运作。我们很自豪能与他们一起工作。我对我们未来可以一起做的事情非常乐观。

与此同时，我们一直诚实地认为这项技术存在非常现实的风险。这些问题包括个人或民族国家滥用技术、经济混乱、失去对人工智能系统的控制等。我们讨论这些风险不是因为我们认为它们是不可避免的，而是因为我们认为它们是可以避免的。

避免它们取决于构建人工智能的人们做出的选择。如果我们不关心安全，人工智能将会如何发展，而如果我们痴迷于安全，人工智能将会如何发展，两者之间存在着巨大的差异。对安全和公共利益的痴迷从一开始就融入了 Anthropic 的基因中。从防范生物和网络风险，到校准训练和测试，再到像 X 射线一样观察我们的模型，Anthropic 开创了理解和引导人工智能系统行为的方法。

任重而道远，最艰巨的安全工作还在后面。该公司拥有令人难以置信的人才，使我们能够构建最强大的人工智能系统，我们需要对其进行双重和三重检查，以确保这些人工智能系统的安全性，甚至比现在更加努力。

明确地说，我们将加快人工智能系统的训练和部署步伐，只要有必要，我们就确信它们是安全的，并将继续处于人类控制之下。我们不会屈服于商业或政治压力。今天，公司的财务状况变得更加强大，这样做只会增强我们做正确事情的决心。

如果我们能够证明我们可以在安全方面做出正确的选择，同时仍能打造一家极其成功的公司，那么我们行业的其他人也会受到启发，采取同样的做法。我们称之为登顶竞赛。当竞争顺利进行时，哪家公司拥有最好的模型并不重要——每个人都会赢，因为每个人都在安全地建造。当处于领先地位时，通往顶峰的竞争效果最好，我们完全希望并期望这样做，但目标是让整个行业变得更好，无论 Anthropic 在任何特定时间是赢还是输。

机器智能的出现是人类历史上的开创性时刻之一，我们有一个难得的机会来让它变得更好。

这一刻比任何一家公司或任何一个国家都重要。我们所有人都需要共同努力，才能确保这项技术为我们和子孙后代带来良好的发展。从今天开始，我们希望您能加入我们的行列。

Adding to the post attached, @RBI must also immediately create a policy around the use of AI agents in operating Indian bank accounts.

If a customer uses AI agents to access and work with their account, the bank must not be held responsible for hacks or issues arising out of it.

It must work something like this:

- Indian banks must be asked to build measures to detect the use of AI agents accessing accounts and flag the customer.

- The bank, at this moment, does not know if the customer is using the AI agent themselves or it is an unauthorized agent. 

- So they must suspend operations on the account and send a notice to the customer informing of the same. 

- The bank must ask them to accept an agreement waiving liability if they chose to use AI agents. 

- If the customer doesn't agree, then the bank must block all AI agents accessing the accounts of the customer. 

In fact, it may be a good idea to temporarily block all AI agent access to all Indian bank accounts until better measures and security is in place.

Just heard of someone's account getting drained because of an AI agent they had deployed themselves. Now, why should deposit insurance or the bank be responsible for this?

viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_en:
Excited to announce the Sakana AI Security Research Group, an independent, public-interest R&D team in Tokyo co-led by Akihiro Umegai and me.

Cybersecurity has become a critical national priority for Japan as AI changes the speed and economics of both offense and defense. Rather than endlessly chasing patches downstream, we are approaching security as an upstream quality engineering problem, something Japan has long been strong at. We are also researching collective multi-agent defense and how to secure AI agents themselves.

We will be publishing our research, reproducible benchmarks, and practical playbooks openly, while working closely with partners across government, industry, and academia.

Full English post here: https://t.co/HnofMjQTa3

We're hiring researchers in Tokyo to help shape the group's agenda across systems reliability and AI agent security: https://t.co/sF9ydogvFD

top_three.title_en: California AG subpoenas Nvidia over Jensen Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
top_three.author: Katie Nicora

top_three.summary_en: President Donald Trump dismissed National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, with DoD CIO Kirsten Davies serving as interim lead. The move follows widespread technical outages that crippled U.S. air travel and banking sectors, prompting intense legislative scrutiny over the administration's crisis response capabilities.
paragraphs: WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross was "fired" from his job, a person close to the White House said on Thursday, days after technology outages disrupted US air travel, banking and national security systems.

The ouster comes as US President Donald Trump and his administration face mounting scrutiny over their response to the series of disruptions over the past week, including a global outage affecting hundreds of millions of Microsoft users and a nationwide halt to air travel that disrupted more than 18,000 flights.
The dismissal of Cairncross dismissal is the administration's first major personnel move since the outages.

Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source.
"The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position," said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Cairncross said in a statement on Thursday night it was the "honor of a lifetime to serve" in Trump's administration.

The recent technology disruptions are likely linked to corporate efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered software vulnerabilities in the AI age, cybersecurity experts told Reuters. Advanced AI tools make it easier for companies to uncover weaknesses in their cybersecurity protections.
The top US intelligence official said on Wednesday the disruptions were separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.

Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri on Tuesday told reporters in Washington the Trump administration should brief lawmakers on the outages so they can "share with the American people what's happening here."

Cairncross was an executive at the Republican National Committee before assuming the cyber director role. His successor will need to be confirmed by the US Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.

Ally 的条款称，客户“对人工智能采取的任何行动负责”。

从 11 月 24 日起，富国银行将要求客户对代理人的行为承担责任，即使他们要求代理人停止，除非他们能够证明他们撤销了代理人的访问权限。

埃隆·马斯克 (Elon Musk) 对他的 Grok Bot 代理做出了相反的承诺：如果出现问题，“我们会让你变得完整。” Grok 自己的条款仍然要求用户负责。
linked_tweets.content_en:
‼️ Major US banks are telling customers that when their AI agent makes a mistake with their money, they're on the hook.

Ally's terms say customers are "responsible for any actions that the AI takes."

From 24 November, Wells Fargo will hold customers liable for what an agent does even after they tell it to stop, unless they can prove they revoked its access.

Elon Musk promises the opposite for his Grok Bot agent: if it messes up, "we will make you whole." Grok's own terms still make users responsible.

news.title: Anthropic Slumps 5% Post-Market After Record $107.3 Billion IPO
news.title_en: Anthropic Slumps 5% Post-Market After Record $107.3 Billion IPO
news.title_zh: Anthropic创纪录1073亿美元IPO上市首日收涨后，盘后股价回撤约5%
news.author: Natasha Mascarenhas, Carmen Reinicke, and Sangmi Cha
news.image_caption: Anthropic PBC signage during the company's initial public offering at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, on Nov. 19. (John Lamparski / Bloomberg)
news.summary_zh: 人工智能初创公司Anthropic以1073亿美元估值完成IPO，上市首日盘后股价回撤约5%
news.summary_en: AI developer Anthropic PBC saw its shares decline by approximately 5% in post-market trading following a record-breaking $107.3 billion IPO. The stock had previously gained 17% during its debut, reflecting strong investor appetite for the maker of Claude, though broader market volatility eventually weighed on its performance.
news.lead_paragraph: Anthropic PBC shares were down about 5% in post-market trading as the artificial intelligence developer wrapped up its first day as a public company after a record-setting $107.3 billion offering.
news.lead_paragraph_zh: Anthropic PBC 的股价在盘后交易中下跌约 5%，这家人工智能开发商在创纪录的 1073 亿美元发行后结束了上市首日交易。
paragraphs: Anthropic PBC shares were down about 5% in post-market trading as the artificial intelligence developer wrapped up its first day as a public company after a record-setting $107.3 billion offering.

The late moves pared a debut pop of 17% on Thursday, which provided a rare bright spot as the Nasdaq fell 2.2%. The broader market continued on a downward trend into the Asian day, with global stocks poised for their longest losing streak in more than three years, as the AI trade cratered.

While the bright open for the Claude chatbot maker reflected massive investor appetite after a heavily oversubscribed initial public offering, the late slide underscored the volatility facing tech megacaps amidst shifting expectations for enterprise software monetization and high capital expenditure.

Anthropic priced its offering at $83 a share, above an already elevated target range, raising more than $8.1 billion in new proceeds. Backed by major technology giants including Amazon.com Inc. and Alphabet Inc., the company has emerged alongside OpenAI as a linchpin of generative AI infrastructure.

Trading in Anthropic's shares drew intense scrutiny across Wall Street as analysts evaluated whether monumental frontier model development and GPU computing costs can yield sustained profitability. The IPO represents the largest venture-backed tech listing in history, surpassing previous records set by high-profile cloud and social media debuts.
paragraphs_zh: Anthropic PBC 的股价在盘后交易中下跌约 5%，这家人工智能开发商在创纪录的 1073 亿美元发行后结束了上市首日交易。
周四的尾盘走势回吐了 17% 的首日涨幅，为纳斯达克指数下跌 2.2% 提供了难得的亮点。随着人工智能交易的暴跌，大盘继续呈下跌趋势，进入亚洲交易日，全球股市将出现三年多以来最长的连续下跌。
虽然 Claude 聊天机器人开发商在开盘时的强劲表现反映了经历严重超额认购后投资者的巨大热情，但尾盘的回落凸显了大型科技企业面临的市场波动——在企业级软件商业化变现与庞大资本开支周期的交织下，市场情绪正经历剧烈博弈。
Anthropic 将 IPO 发行价定为每股 83 美元，高于此前已上调的指导区间上限，单笔募资超 81 亿美元。在亚马逊（Amazon.com Inc.）与 Alphabet Inc. 等科技巨头的巨额注资背书下，Anthropic 已与 OpenAI 并列成为全球生成式 AI 基础设施的核心支柱。
Anthropic 的挂牌交易引发了华尔街投行的全方位审视，分析师聚焦于前沿大模型研发与 GPU 算力集群的庞大资本开支能否转化为可持续的盈利能力。此次上市创下了全球风险投资支持科技企业史上规模最大的 IPO 纪录，打破了此前所有云计算与移动互联网巨头保持的公开发行市值高度。
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】Anthropic PBC（人工智能开发商）在纳斯达克交易所（Nasdaq）：完成1073亿美元估值IPO，首日盘后股价回撤5%
【起因与机理】全球股市整体疲软及AI板块估值回调压力
【关键数据与实测】Anthropic以1073亿美元估值完成IPO并挂牌交易，发行价83美元募资超81亿美元。
【行业影响与走向】受全球股市下行周期及AI概念板块整体波动影响，二级市场对算力变现高度敏感。
fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] Anthropic PBC (AI Developer) (Nasdaq): Completed $107.3 billion IPO; shares fell 5% post-market
[Root Cause & Mechanism] Broader market decline and correction in AI sector valuations
[Key Metrics] Anthropic went public with a $107.3 billion valuation at $83 per share, raising over $8.1 billion.
[Key Position & Outlook] Driven by broader global market downturn and cooling sentiment toward AI stocks.

news.title: California AG subpoenas Nvidia over Jensen Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
news.title_en: California AG subpoenas Nvidia over Jensen Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
news.author: Katie Nicora
news.content_snippet:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced an investigative subpoena on chipmaker Nvidia on Thursday following allegations the company's former CEO and co-founder, Jensen Huang, had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

In a press release, Bonta said that the California Department of Justice was investigating whether Nvidia's advanced chips or confidential information were obtained by China. The probe also seeks to determine if Nvidia misled investors and the public, as well as whether t
news.summary_en: California Attorney General Rob Bonta has issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia to assess whether the personal conduct of former CEO Jensen Huang facilitated the unauthorized transfer of advanced chip technologies or confidential intelligence to Chinese entities. The investigation focuses on potential violations of state securities laws and failure to adequately disclose material risks to investors.

news.title: Commerce approved sales of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies, Rep. Mast says
news.title_en: Commerce approved sales of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies, Rep. Mast says
news.author: Justin Papp and Katie Tarasov
news.content_snippet:
The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies,"according to the documents. From December through
news.summary_en: Documents released by the U.S. House Foreign Affairs Committee reveal that the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) approved the export of over 879,000 AI chips to Chinese firms including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, with some recipients flagged by the Department of Defense as Chinese Military Companies. While Nvidia and AMD assert compliance with export control laws, Representative Gregory Meeks criticized the administration's enforcement efficacy, prompting congressional oversight into current regulatory policies.

news.author: Reuters
news.content_snippet:
WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross was "fired" from his job, a person close to the White House said on Thursday, days after technology outages disrupted US air travel, banking and national security systems.

The ouster comes as US President Donald Trump and his administration face mounting scrutiny over their response to the series of disruptions over the past week, including a global outage affecting hundreds of millions of Microsoft users and a n
news.summary_en: President Donald Trump dismissed National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, with DoD CIO Kirsten Davies serving as interim lead. The move follows widespread technical outages that crippled U.S. air travel and banking sectors, prompting intense legislative scrutiny over the administration's crisis response capabilities.
paragraphs: WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross was "fired" from his job, a person close to the White House said on Thursday, days after technology outages disrupted US air travel, banking and national security systems.

The ouster comes as US President Donald Trump and his administration face mounting scrutiny over their response to the series of disruptions over the past week, including a global outage affecting hundreds of millions of Microsoft users and a nationwide halt to air travel that disrupted more than 18,000 flights.
The dismissal of Cairncross dismissal is the administration's first major personnel move since the outages.

Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source.
"The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position," said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Cairncross said in a statement on Thursday night it was the "honor of a lifetime to serve" in Trump's administration.

The recent technology disruptions are likely linked to corporate efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered software vulnerabilities in the AI age, cybersecurity experts told Reuters. Advanced AI tools make it easier for companies to uncover weaknesses in their cybersecurity protections.
The top US intelligence official said on Wednesday the disruptions were separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.

Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri on Tuesday told reporters in Washington the Trump administration should brief lawmakers on the outages so they can "share with the American people what's happening here."

Cairncross was an executive at the Republican National Committee before assuming the cyber director role. His successor will need to be confirmed by the US Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.

paragraphs: Menlo Ventures and Spark Capital are two such firms emerging with some of the biggest returns by multiple
FOR decades, venture capital thrived on small bets that became billion-dollar companies.
Then came Anthropic, rewriting the playbook and forcing investors to write fatter checks to buy stakes at unheard-of valuations.

The artificial intelligence lab’s shares began trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday (Nov 19) at a US$1.5 trillion valuation, delivering multibillion-dollar windfalls to venture investors at a moment when the industry needs fresh liquidity to fund more bets on AI companies.
The stock closed at US$97.17, up 17 per cent from its initial public offering price of US$83.
Anthropic’s stock market value ended the day at about US$1.3 trillion, based on its outstanding shares, or US$1.8 trillion, based on its fully diluted shares.
To join the fundraising frenzy, especially at later stages, venture capital firms invested billions, tapping their own investors for additional capital through special-purpose vehicles.

Menlo Ventures and Spark Capital emerged with some of the biggest returns by multiple.

Spark Capital was the first venture capital firm to lead an Anthropic investment, in a US$450 million Series C round in 2023 at a valuation of US$4.5 billion. Spark general partner Yasmin Razavi, who spearheaded the investment, remains the only investor who sits on Anthropic’s board.

Writing the largest check in the firm’s history, early-stage firm Menlo invested over US$1 billion for a stake of nearly 1.5 per cent, according to a person familiar with the investment. At a US$1.5 trillion market cap, Menlo’s stake is worth over US$20 billion.

To invest beyond the capacity of its existing fund, Menlo raised a US$750 million special-purpose vehicle from limited partners, a tactic that became increasingly common as funding rounds grew, given the capital needs of AI companies.
Sequoia Capital, long known for its early bets, joined a later round and still stands to earn billions of dollars.

Sequoia passed on Anthropic at lower prices. After a leadership change, it wrote its first check at the start of this year, joining a round led by Singapore’s GIC and Coatue at a US$380 billion post-money valuation in February.

It later co-led, alongside Altimeter, Dragoneer and Greenoaks, a round at US$965 billion. Sequoia has invested US$3 billion in Anthropic and continued to invest more through Anthropic’s IPO, signalling further conviction in the AI lab.

Lightspeed Venture Partners, which invested more than US$3 billion in Anthropic, now holds over 2 per cent of the company, making it the largest financial investor in the company, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The returns are possible because of the rapid rise in Anthropic’s valuation and revenue. Its annualised revenue grew from about US$1 billion at the start of 2025 to about US$81 billion last month, as its valuation climbed from US$61.5 billion in March 2025 to US$965 billion in the latest private round this May.
Strategic backers, too, supply much of the unprecedented capital and computing power needed by AI labs. The combined stake of Amazon and Alphabet’s Google in Anthropic is about 28.4 per cent.

Will Griffith, a partner at Iconiq, said: “We’re living through a very unique time of profound change happening at a higher velocity than ever before. The scale of the impact of these businesses and the breadth of market opportunities is larger than anything we’ve seen before.
“And that is going to afford investment opportunities that are larger than what we’ve seen in the past.”
He has invested US$6.1 billion, making the fund the second-largest financial investor by ownership in Anthropic. REUTERS

news.summary_en: Apple is pivoting its AI strategy by recruiting for a 'Proactive, Agentic AI' engineering lead to develop autonomous systems capable of cross-app interaction, code debugging, and complex task planning. The initiative, integrating teams from Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models, aims to move beyond static voice commands toward an autonomous agent environment capable of multi-step execution across devices.
paragraphs: Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That’s according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant.

An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhonemaker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet, and Google’s Tasks. Muse, ChatGPT, and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps, while Google just started letting Gemini do the same.

Apple began rolling out its AI-upgraded Siri in September, which you can use to ask questions about what’s on your screen, as well as perform actions across apps. It looks like Apple is planning to give Siri more agentic capabilities, as a report from Bloomberg suggests the company could add the ability to rotate and crop images in Photos, or organize Safari tabs. This lines up with the company’s new job listing, which says the engineer will work closely with teams across its Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models divisions.

“People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service,” the job listing says. “We’re building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.”

With its upcoming iOS 27.3 update, Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into “all apps.” This is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps.

paragraphs: Bloomberg reports that Apple is hiring engineers to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of browsing the web, writing code, and controlling apps on behalf of users. Here are the details.
### Apple working on AI agent that can code, browse the web, more

In a report published today, Bloomberg notes that new job listings on Apple’s website indicate the company’s efforts to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of performing complex tasks on the user’s behalf.
Since the breakout success of OpenClaw, autonomous AI agents have become increasingly popular, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and SpaceXSI among those offering their own solutions.
The increasing popularity of these agents has put Apple under pressure to catch up, while the company has also introduced new restrictions on how third-party AI agents can access and control Macs.

Last month, Apple announced plans to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access, with changes introduced in the macOS 27.3 beta that give users more granular control over which apps and information third-party AI agents can access.

Over at the App Store, Meta’s Muse has become one of the fastest-growing apps in US history, surpassing 10 million downloads in just 40 days, according to Sensor Tower, and spending weeks at the top of the charts. As of today, it sits at No. 2 among free apps, behind TikTok.

And while there are differences in how phone-based and computer-based agents operate, these systems can usually work together, coordinating tasks across devices and apps to accomplish increasingly complex goals.
Back to Bloomberg’s report, it notes Apple recently posted new job listings that offer a closer look at its plans to develop autonomous AI agents:

In one, Apple said it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.
One job listing, which is for “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” features the following summary:

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”

The listing also notes that Apple is building agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way,” much like existing solutions from frontier AI labs.

Today’s report on the new job listings comes just days after Bloomberg reported that Apple wants to make Siri more like an autonomous AI agent, with the ability to proactively carry out tasks without requiring users to initiate every step. According to Mark Gurman, the company could introduce these capabilities as soon as next year.
With the new job listings, Apple has offered a more detailed look at its plans for autonomous AI agents, although the language suggests that development is still in its early stages.

Of course, given how quickly the technology is evolving, the landscape could look very different by the time Apple is ready to introduce its own solution next year, much like how the industry had already moved toward autonomous agents by the time Apple finally launched its long-awaited Siri AI overhaul.

news.summary_en: Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang resigned following misconduct allegations, causing the stock to drop nearly 40% from its October 6th peak, despite a record-breaking Q3 revenue of $115.8 billion and the rapid shipment of the Vera Rubin platform. Chairman Harvey Jones has confirmed that the board will not reinstate Huang and has initiated an executive search to stabilize leadership.
paragraphs: “We’ve got this,” Colette Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia, said Tuesday night as she closed out the embattled chip company’s third quarter earnings call.

By Thursday, the company’s stock price was hovering at around $150 per share, a nearly 40 percent drop from its all-time high on October 6th, and wiping out a brief post-earnings pop on Tuesday night. Meanwhile, Wall Street was paying up for one of Nvidia’s biggest customers as Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut at $111.50 per share — 34 percent higher than expected.

Looking at the earnings report numbers alone, Nvidia had a blockbuster quarter. Q3 revenue more than doubled from the same period last year up to total $115.8 billion, driven by data center revenue that was up 110 percent and exceeding Wall Street expectations. Nearly $20 billion in revenue came from the highly anticipated Vera Rubin platform, which shipped during the quarter, becoming the “fastest product ramp in company history,” Kress told investors.

“Our momentum is real,” Kress said. “With the market-leading multiyear roadmap, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade, and sustainable demand, we are well positioned to accelerate Nvidia’s leadership position.”
But investors are stilltrying to reconcile Nvidia’s stellar recent financial performance and position as a central pillar in the AI economy with serious concerns over its future.

The company’s stock has taken a stunning tumble in recent weeks. Fueled first by a broader market sell-off of chip stocks amid concerns about the AI bubble, the stock took another blow following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, according to US intelligence sources cited by The New York Times.

Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s newly appointed chairman of the board, told investors on the call Tuesday that the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and has already tapped an executive search firm to help find a replacement. Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and has led the company ever since — famously without a succession plan — has become essentially inseparable from it in the eyes of Wall Street and the media. But while Huang may not be ready to let go, posting on X this week that he’d be “honored” to be reinstated as CEO, Nvidia’s executive suite seems ready to move on.
It has been a tumultuous two and a half weeks for Nvidia.

On October 29th, The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies believed Jensen Huang to be the target of a Chinese espionage plot. The report centered on his “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company and one of Nvidia’s clients. Nvidia initially contested the report, adding that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang “are not unusual or unexpected.”

Nvidia’s stock seemingly remained unaffected by the reports, at least at first. The share price closed at $213.66 on October 29th, down just 0.8 percent from the previous day. (Julian Barnes, one of the reporters on the story, later commented, “I will confess I was kind of surprised that the world’s initial reaction to our October story was a bit muted.”) The stock closed at a 4 percent drop the next day as the entire Nasdaq fell 2.9 percent, the worst single-day decline since June.

The stock continued to fall through Wednesday, November 4th, the day after the blue wave swept the midterms, stoking fears on Wall Street that the new class of Democratic governors in key states like Texas would slow down data center construction. On Thursday, November 5th, Nvidia’s stock fell 9.2 percent, its largest single-day drop in at least a year. But chip stocks began to recover the next day, and by close on Friday, November 6th, Nvidia was back up 2.8 percent to a share price of $186.64.

Then all hell broke loose. On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang sent a company-wide memo to Nvidia staff in which he apologized for engaging in an extramarital affair. The memo coincided with the opening of an independent investigation by Nvidia’s board into Huang’s alleged misconduct and whether company secrets or national security had been compromised. Huang said he would cooperate fully with the investigation. By the opening bell on Monday, November 9th, Nvidia shares had tumbled 7 percent and trading volume surged past its three-month average as investors reacted to the memo. After a brief rebound, the stock continued to oscillate the next day, as more details of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang’s relationship emerged. By the time the market closed on Tuesday, November 10th, Nvidia shares were down to $168.89, nearly 10 percent below the closing price on the last day of 2025.

The stock rebounded slightly on Wednesday, November 11th, as investors prepared for Nvidia’s third quarter earnings call, scheduled for the following Tuesday, November 17th. By Wednesday night, however, shares had plunged yet again as media reports circulated that Nvidia’s board was considering ousting Huang, and other reports emerged detailing a second alleged affair, this time between Huang and an Nvidia employee.

Nvidia announced Huang’s departure on the morning of Thursday, November 12th, sending the company’s shares falling nearly 14 percent at the open. It closed at just a 4.3 percent dip. The intraday low of $148.80 per share was its lowest price in a year.

On December 1st, Jensen Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee for transcribed interviews. Nvidia’s general counsel will do the same on December 2nd.

Retail investors have already seized the opportunity to buy the dip. In the first 30 minutes of trading on Thursday, November 12th, retail investors bought $111 million of Nvidia shares in the largest-ever first half-hour of opening for the stock, Bloomberg reported, citing Vanda Research.
They might be onto something.
Nvidia’s average price target is $232.59, with the lowest estimate at $130 and the highest at $350, according to an analysis of analyst projections over the last three months by Google Finance.
Nearly two-thirds of those analysts issued a “Buy” rating for Nvidia in the last three months. Of those, all 30 reiterated that rating post-earnings.
The stock closed at $145.98 on Thursday, a new 52-week low.

Then again, numbers are the core basis for stock market ratings, and numbers may not be Nvidia’s problem right now. It’s everything else — the leadership vacuum, upcoming congressional testimony, regulatory uncertainty, broader questions about neocloud customer financing and sales to China — that will continue to impact the stock in the coming weeks.

news.title: What’s With All These Outages?
news.title_en: What’s With All These Outages?
news.author: Brian Barrett, Leah Feiger, and Sophie Kleeman
news.content_snippet: Microsoft, the FAA, Chase, United, the NSA, and Apple all went down within one week. Officials say none of the outages were cyberattacks, but the internet isn’t buying it. This week on Uncanny Valley, WIRED senior business editor Sophie Kleeman joins Brian Barrett and Leah Feiger to discuss what actually went wrong and why people jumped straight to blaming hackers and AI. Plus, Anthropic’s historic IPO at a reported $1.5 trillion, Nvidia’s first earnings report since Jensen Huang resigned, and t
news.summary_en: Major infrastructure outages occurred sequentially at Microsoft, the FAA, JPMorgan Chase, United Airlines, the NSA, and Apple. Despite official denials of cyberattacks, market anxiety is mounting due to the convergence of these failures with Anthropic's reported $1.5 trillion IPO plans, the first Nvidia earnings report post-Jensen Huang's resignation, and new US executive orders aimed at restricting Chinese entities from accessing AI compute via cloud rentals.
paragraphs: Microsoft, the FAA, Chase, United, the NSA, and Apple all went down within one week. Officials say none of the outages were cyberattacks, but the internet isn’t buying it. This week on Uncanny Valley, WIRED senior business editor Sophie Kleeman joins Brian Barrett and Leah Feiger to discuss what actually went wrong and why people jumped straight to blaming hackers and AI. Plus, Anthropic’s historic IPO at a reported $1.5 trillion, Nvidia’s first earnings report since Jensen Huang resigned, and the administration’s new rule to stop Chinese companies from renting AI chips just before Trump meets Xi.
Articles mentioned in this episode:
You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Sophie Kleeman on X/Twitter at @sophiekleeman, and Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger. Write to us at [email protected].

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.
Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Brian Barrett: Hey, this is Brian. If you've been listening for a while and you haven't rated or reviewed the podcast yet, this is your sign. Give us a rating, tell us what you think. Five stars is nice, but we'll take the feedback too. It really helps more people find the show. OK, onto the show. So hey everybody, I want to say first of all, we've got a very special guest today in the studio with Leah. It's Sophie Kleeman.
Leah Feiger: Woo-hoo. Sophie's here.
Sophie Kleeman: I'm here.

Brian Barrett: Sophie is our senior editor on the business desk and we're so glad to have her. And I've heard that she is going to do a lot of yelling and pointing and just anger I think is her vibe, is what I've been told, coming in.
Sophie Kleeman: Yes. Let's get started.
Brian Barrett: Welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I'm Brian Barrett, executive editor.
Leah Feiger: I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science.
Sophie Kleeman: And I am Sophie Kleeman, senior business editor.

Brian Barrett: This week we're discussing why everything seems to be breaking down all the time. First, it was Microsoft, then the FAA and air traffic control. Then Chase Bank, United Airlines, the NSA, Apple, the tech outages have been piling up and raising questions around what caused them, and why they're happening all at the same time seemingly. Secretary of State Marco Rubio says that we are not under attack. He's right, but the internet is not convinced. We'll get into what actually went wrong, and why a lot of people's first instinct is to blame hackers and AI in some combination.

Sophie Kleeman: And I am one of those people, so can't wait to get into that. We will also take a look at Anthropic officially going public this week. It will be one of the biggest IPOs ever, but the timing is a little bit complicated. So we will talk about who's about to get very, very rich and whether the recent midterm results could impact the company's grand ambitions.

Brian Barrett: And in other AI news, we're going to have a quick NVIDIA update as the company just released the first earnings report without Jensen Huang at the helm and had their first all hands led by interim CEO Colette Kress.

Leah Feiger: We're also going to be checking in on President Donald Trump's visit to Asia, specifically China, which comes just days after his administration has moved to close a loophole that lets Chinese companies access AI chips. We're going to talk about what the NVIDIA scandal has had to do with all of this and the fight inside the administration over how to handle everything.

Brian Barrett: All right look, if you picked up your phone at any point in last week to look at the news, if you went to wired.com at any point last week or anywhere on social media, you were hit with news that something somewhere had an outage.
Leah Feiger: Brian, everything is broken.
Brian Barrett: Everything's broken.
Leah Feiger: Every single thing is broken.

Brian Barrett: Everything's broken and breaking, increasingly fixed. I want to walk through this really quickly. I know people are tired of it, the so many things. We're going to list off some of the biggest ones, OK? Last Thursday, Microsoft had an outage in Outlook and Teams that was about 24 hours, which is incredibly long for those services to be out when the whole world basically depends on them to communicate. The next day, Friday, the FAA had a ground stop for the entire country, only the second time that has happened since 9/11, and it was the longest one since then. It was for more than four hours. Then on Monday, everyone said that their banks no longer worked. It turns out to be JP Morgan Chase specifically had a problem, but because banks are all counterparties to each other, every bank had an issue. If one bank had an issue, that same day, United delayed more than a hundred flights for a separate issue. Then on Tuesday, the NSA's classified internal network went down and just for good measure, an internal update also knocked out iCloud and Apple Pay for not quite as long, not quite as dramatically, but throw it on the pile. Now I want to be clear, every single one of these companies and agencies and organizations has said the incidents were not cyberattacks. It was not some combination of a ruthless AI agent and Iranian hackers. There's no evidence that any of these clustered tech failures were even related aside from the bank thing, which is self-contained in the banking industry, but that hasn't stopped people from being suspicious, trying to find a through line, and I think getting on their conspiracy horses. And Sophie, you've been riding one at the front of the battle.
Sophie Kleeman: Yes, I sure have.
Brian Barrett: Yeah. How are you taking all of this in so I can debunk it?
Sophie Kleeman: OK. So I would like to say first off that I do think this has sort of trickled down into people who don't follow this super closely.
Leah Feiger: I mean, it had to. This was your emails, this was your banking, these were your flights.
Sophie Kleeman: Right. Everyone's talking about this.
Leah Feiger: This is it.

Sophie Kleeman: To give you two very, very, very distinct examples, yesterday my fantasy football group chat blew up because someone was like, "Hey guys who follow this, and who are paying attention, are we under attack?" And Brian, you'll be proud of me. I actually said you should read wired.com for the answer to that.
Brian Barrett: Good job, Sophie.
Leah Feiger: She did not say, "Yes, go to the bunkers." Which I know is what you wanted to say.
Sophie Kleeman: It is what I wanted to say.

Leah Feiger: Look, I will say though, I get that inclination. These are so many public services that everyone has really just taken for granted, not only to work, but to help us function in our day-to-day lives. I talked to friends who were like, "Oh yeah, I just had a day and a half off of work basically, and then could not pay my rent." It was everything.

Brian Barrett: And there are people who are doing doomsday prepping at Costco now. I've had multiple group chats where people, even when I've told them, "Hey, it's actually fine," they are still prepping their bunkers. I think it's instructive. I have covered outages for a long time at WIRED because I think they're fascinating because they affect so many people, and they have such mundane causes usually. So I want to talk through a couple of things and what happened. Just for any listeners who are still worried about it, they all have very distinct things. The Microsoft Outlook issue was actually ... I love this one. It was a fix that was deployed in July. They basically made an update in July, propagated it out, but was not triggered until last week. Something else happened.
Sophie Kleeman: Do we know what that something else is? I'm just asking questions.

Brian Barrett: Iranian hackers. No, they've done a shorter postmortem. They're going to do a longer postmortem. The gist of it was they pushed this thing out and then it propagated out through the whole network and then they had another update. They stepped on the landmine and everything went boom, and it took a while to correct. For the FAA, when air traffic control went down, and Aarian Marshall, who covers transportation mobility for us here at WIRED, was very early to say this doesn't seem like hackers. There was a lot of suspicion there because the FAA just the day before had rolled out an AI system to help with air traffic control. The difference is that system's more about data, and about where planes are going and what they're doing. The system that was affected, the problem on Friday, was that people couldn't talk to each other. It was a comms issue. And that tied back to old, old, old fiber equipment that a company called L3Harris maintains. They were trying to push an update on Friday afternoon, which you never do. That's the crazy part to me is that they were trying to push—
Leah Feiger: It's the perfect time.
Sophie Kleeman: Yeah.
Brian Barrett: Push an update to production on a Friday, a couple weeks before Thanksgiving? Crazy stuff.

Leah Feiger: And then I mean the rest was all the same too, right Brian? Chase blamed a software bug in their own hardware. United said it was a technology related issue. NSA blamed routine maintenance. Apple blamed an internal update. All of this was kind of the same. It was just all happening at the same time.
Sophie Kleeman: At the same time.

Leah Feiger: But I think I get it. I get the fears here. I also understand the timing in some ways. We're nearing the end of the year. People need to push all of these updates before holiday travel season or just holiday banking season, I guess, email season.
Sophie Kleeman: Email season.

Leah Feiger: But it is understandable that everyone went straight to the hackers, straight to AI overlords because we've actually been having a not small amount of those examples. If you had told me that this was another Hugging Face incident, I would've been like, yep. Alright. Sounds good.
Sophie Kleeman: You're like, yeah, that sounds right.

Brian Barrett: Well, and Leah too, I think what doesn't help, there's the political dimension here too, because Markwayne Mullin can tell me everything's fine, all he wants. I don't necessarily buy anything from him.
Sophie Kleeman: I don't believe him.
Brian Barrett: Right. I inherently, this administration has no credibility. So in these moments, what do we do?

Leah Feiger: I have to shout out our podcast producer right now. Obviously we are sitting here with a list of notes about all of this and I just quickly looked at it and one tab line was, also people don't trust the government.
Sophie Kleeman: Incredible.

Leah Feiger: Which is, yeah, that is the situation right now. That is perhaps the most succinct, accurate way to push this, which is there was just a massive referendum a few weeks ago. Dems are coming in, guns blazing, and everything is breaking right before that happens. I get it.

Sophie Kleeman: I'm the devil's advocate here, right? I was the person last week where I was like, we're all going to die. We're under attack. This is crazy. This is all happening at the same time. Obviously I don't think that that's really the case, but I will say that I do think two things. I think people are quick to blame AI for things because they don't like it, they don't understand it, they are scared of it, and the companies who are selling it are not doing a great job of selling their product in ways that make people want to sort of feel good about themselves. But the second point is that it was AI, right? It was just the flip side of it. It was like, these companies are deploying these incredibly advanced systems to find vulnerabilities, to find issues within their very complex and in some cases old systems and they're finding it and then they're patching it all at the same time. And that's what I think that reporting has suggested that's what we're seeing.

Brian Barrett: This goes back to Anthropic's Mythos model, which is very good at cybersecurity. You might remember it from such news headlines as Anthropic gets banned from the Pentagon and other stupid moments in AI history. Mythos is very, very good at cybersecurity. Anthropic gave access to a limited number, actually a decent number of people who control sensitive information, governments, organizations, companies, and those companies have since been using it to identify bugs that they couldn't find otherwise. Sending patches at a huge rate, and the more complicated the bug, the more patches trying to push out at the same time, the more likely something is going to break. And I think that's what we're seeing here. So yeah, AI plays a role, but in some ways you can think of this as companies trying to get ahead of the hacking version of this. They're doing this because otherwise, in a few months, someone's going to actually say, oh, we can break into the air traffic control system, shut it down ourselves.
Sophie Kleeman: Am I the only one who would love to see that? What if we just went offline forever? What if it all shut down? That would be great. We could all touch grass.
Brian Barrett: I think that'd be great.
Sophie Kleeman: Finally.
Leah Feiger: All right.
Brian Barrett: I think it'd be great.
Sophie Kleeman: Thank you Brian.
Brian Barrett: It would affect the podcast, but that's OK. We can mail each other letters.

Leah Feiger: I've been tickled though by all of these comments from our government officials. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has tried really hard to kind of deescalate this as well, claiming there's no foul play. He's traveling with Trump in Asia this week and he said in a press conference multiple times, "We are not under systemic attack."

Marco Rubio, archival audio: The first thing I want to make very clear is that we have zero evidence whatsoever. We have no indication, no evidence, and no reason to believe at all that any of these incidents are related to each other.
Leah Feiger: And Trump had a different take. I was slightly less reassured.
Archival audio: Are you concerned about all these outages? Microsoft, the FAA, United, Chase Bank?
Donald Trump, archival audio: No. It's life. When you're big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It's fine.
Leah Feiger: OK. The reason I had to pivot to that is that's perhaps like the Sophie model here. You're like, "Yeah, shut it down. This is it. This is what we've signed up for."
Sophie Kleeman: You know what? We're just going to roll with it.
Leah Feiger: Sophie and Trump, two peas in a pod.

Sophie Kleeman: We are such similar people in so many ways. In other news, it's been a crazy week, hasn't it? So Anthropic finally arrived on the stock market. The company's long-awaited IPO debut started trading under the ticker ANT, which I would just like to say is actually very cute. And it's valued at a reported one and a half trillion dollars, which is just a staggering, staggering number. It is among the biggest IPOs ever, but it is actually below the $2 trillion figure that was floating around several months ago. And since then, things have shifted even more. NVIDIA lost its CEO and about $2 trillion in market value. And in the midterms, voters overwhelmingly rejected provisions that supported data centers that AI companies need. So given this interesting, interesting timing, what are we looking for?
Brian Barrett: I am looking for a lot of people to become insanely wealthy, even if it's slightly less insanely wealthy than it would've been a couple of months ago.
Sophie Kleeman: Just slightly less.
Brian Barrett: Just slightly, just like a little tiny bit.
Sophie Kleeman: To be clear, $1.5 trillion is still ...

Brian Barrett: It's still generational wealth, but how many generations are we talking about? Trick question. Anthropic doesn't care because they all think we're going to die in the next 10 years or so because of AI. Sophie, I'm curious what you think, because when I think of the Anthropic IPO, which I do every day, every day I'm thinking Anthropic IPO.
Sophie Kleeman: You wake up in the morning and you think Anthropic IPO.

Brian Barrett: I think ANT, ANT, ANT. But it's the first, not the first, it's the biggest pure play AI IPO that we've had and maybe that we're going to have depending on what happens with OpenAI. SpaceX had an IPO recently, but that is a rocket company with an AI company stapled to it. So what do you look for when this company goes public and people can trade on it? How much do we look at it as a bellwether for the industry in general? Not on the first day of trading even, but just in general, how much can we look and say, oh, that's how the AI industry is going?

Sophie Kleeman: I mean, I think it is the bellwether, right? It is the first, it is enormous. It's such a leader in the space. And I think that the interesting thing to me is how much it is connected to the other sort of giants in the space, which is to say Amazon and Google, and a few other companies. I mean, those two firms are themselves going to make a shit ton of money from this IPO. They have, what is it? 15 percent. Amazon will own 15 percent. Google will own nearly 14 percent. Those are huge numbers. So I think just this idea that all the financing is tied together and all of these people are riding on the same rocket ship that may or may not crash onto the surface of the earth.

Brian Barrett: And not just that, but Anthropic, they're like a rent not own approach to data centers. So they've got nearly a trillion dollars of data center commitments that is all going to other companies. It is sort of fueling, whether that's SpaceX or Google. So they are such a symbol of the interdependency of this industry. And again, can't stress this enough, they are pretty sure that AI will destroy everything, and think that their best chance to make a trillion dollars is to build the kind of AI that will destroy everything as fast as they can. It's in their prospectus.

Sophie Kleeman: Only they can prevent mass AI destruction. The other thing I would like to sort of cite here, I feel like with these IPO stories, obviously everyone's sort of focused on the money, and the what does it mean and blah, blah, blah. But one kind of very weird fun fact that I would like to just highlight here is that Sam Bankman-Fried of all of this. He was supposed to make money on this because he was invested in Anthropic, but when he went through his bankruptcy, and all of his legal problems, the government clawed back that investment.
Leah Feiger: Wait, so where are his shares now? Love that.
Sophie Kleeman: They got sold to some people for a very little amount of money and now those people are going to be rich.
Leah Feiger: Oh, that's fun. That's a fun thing to follow.
Sophie Kleeman: Highly recommend checking that out.

Leah Feiger: Yeah. Look, you guys know me. I'm interested in this from a political standpoint. Voters voted against data centers. Politicians won their campaigns by promising that data centers were out across the board. This was bipartisan, this was Republican, this was Democrat. So as Anthropic is entering this space, as other companies, OpenAI, etc., are kind of watching how this goes for them, I'm really curious in the coming months what these investments in data centers is going to mean for them. I wonder if it's going to mean slowdowns. I wonder if any of these newly electeds will actually be able to hold these folks accountable. We're going to see, but there is very much a question mark for me there about what comes next.

Sophie Kleeman: I mean, I think one of the great things for us as journalists too about this IPO is Anthropic will now be a public company. So they are much more accountable and accountable in ways that we can actually dig into and go through their 10Ks and go through their 10Qs and all the rest of it. They're going to have to do earnings calls and all the rest of it, which is great for us because we will have such a better window into how they're actually doing.
Leah Feiger: Oh, it's amazing.
Sophie Kleeman: Such a better window into how they're actually doing.

Leah Feiger: Also, just because they're so tied up, sourcing inside Anthropic is hard. This is a company that is very much kept to themselves, which is why any kernel of information ... When Jacob Coxon, the Anthropic doomer who bounced out and said, "This really is going to all end the world," and he was on, I don't know, every single talk show or podcast available. One, because of what he was saying, but two, because getting information from inside of Anthropic is difficult. So to your point, a hundred percent. The fact that we're going to have more information there is a game change.

Brian Barrett: The one thing I would add, yes, it's great for us as journalists. We're going to get to see and know so much more information. I'm not as excited about Anthropic now being on this quarterly cycle of needing to demonstrate constant growth and earnings, which is a private company you're shielded from a little bit because the incentives that will make AI profitable are not necessarily the incentives that will make humanity more sustainable, but that's fine.
Sophie Kleeman: Who cares about sustainability? Yep.

Brian Barrett: Who cares? We're all going to be podcasting in caves. Speaking of giant AI companies that are having big moments, good or bad, we've got to talk a little bit about Nvidia. If you're sick of it, totally understand. It's been everywhere, but there are some important updates. Some things have happened just in the last day or two that we should touch on at least quickly. On Tuesday, the company reported its most recent earnings, not surprising that they had another big, big quarter, $115.8 billion in revenue. It's more than six billion ahead of expectations. It was Nvidia's first earnings report since Jensen Huang resigned last week after it became public that he had had affairs with a woman suspected of being an asset of Chinese intelligence, and also with at least one of his own direct reports within Nvidia. Over the last few days, we've had a number of Silicon Valley leaders, including, surprise, Elon Musk, campaigning to bring him back. Some have floated the theory that he was set up. Huang himself said in a statement, first statement that he released since this all happened, that he would be honored to return to Nvidia if the board would have him back. Sounds like the board is saying absolutely not. They said that in very clear terms during the earnings call. What do we make of Nvidia in this moment? I should say, too, that we are recording this just after Nvidia's first all hands after Jensen Huang left was led by interim CEO, former CFO, Colette Kress. It's a lot of information. She didn't say much other than, "Hey employees, we're going to give you a lot more money and a lot more stock equity to make you happier so that you don't leave."
Sophie Kleeman: And she kept saying, "We got this," right?
Brian Barrett: She kept saying, “We got this.”
Sophie Kleeman: That was her direct quote, that was her top line, "We're going to be fine. We got this. Do not worry."

Leah Feiger: But so many people just don't think that. I can't stop thinking about what Zoë told us last week, Brian, and the week before. She's been saying this for a while now, just about how Jensen was in such a particular place compared to all of his co-CEOs around Silicon Valley and that he was just not insulated. He was not insulated within his company. He's not the Mark Zuckerberg model at Meta where that guy's not going anywhere. There is just no world where he's getting stripped from his title or responsibilities, which then makes this entire Bring Back Jensen campaign all the more interesting to me, to see Elon Musk and all of these variety of CEOs, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, all of these different people who not even are just kind of quietly commenting on the sidelines, but signing literal petitions saying this. There's an interesting look, at least for me, of the accountability of it all, of is this possible? I guess this is possible. This shouldn't be possible.

Sophie Kleeman: I'm fascinated by this. And Brian, I would love to know what you think is going on here because I sort of though the sharks would be circling in a way, or I thought that they would not want to touch this with a 10-foot pole kind of thing. I mean, I understand that Jensen is just such a sort of crucial part of this ecosystem and Nvidia is such a crucial part of this ecosystem. They've sort of engineered it that way, but I'm curious what you think, what's the vibe? Why are they all coming out so strongly?
Brian Barrett: Oh, because I think that they all see a little bit of themselves in him.
Leah Feiger: He's one of their own.

Brian Barrett: A raconteur, a bad boy about town. And when you are a unique special genius, you should be able to get away with doing whatever else. We talked about this before, it's the idea of separating the art from the artist, but applied to real allegedly scummy behavior, like having sex with a direct report and lying to your board of directors about it. I don't think Jensen's coming back. I'm prepared to be wrong because this industry has done dumber things on shorter timelines, but I do think the board has been so resolute in it. I think Nvidia's going to be fine. This is not a popular take, I think. I think they're going to be fine in the long term. They've got such lock in. They've got customers that don't have anywhere else to turn, and it will be a long time before they do. They may not be as essential a pillar to the US economy and the industry in the long run. Maybe they don't grow quite as fast, but I think that's probably healthy overall. I think a smaller Nvidia with more competition is probably ... I mean, it makes less systemic risk for everybody else. So I think we're going to be OK.

Leah Feiger: One more piece of news before we go to break. President Donald Trump is in Asia this week. He stopped in the Philippines. He's heading to China. He's expected to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping on Thursday. Right before the trip, the administration said it was moving forward with a new rule that would clamp down on China's ability to access advanced AI chips through the use of data centers outside of China's borders. The rule aims to close what a lot of folks in Washington thought was a loophole, basically, which is that Chinese firms are banned from buying the most advanced AI chips made by companies like Nvidia, but they have continued to legally access the chips by renting them from data centers. And this issue became the entire issue this past week because of Nvidia, because Alice Huang was an executive at one of these companies, Megaspeed. WIRED senior correspondent Hugo Lowell has been reporting on what the administration's response has been throughout all of this. And it's been really interesting, honestly, which is for as much as Trump and co are like, "We have to be ahead of China. This is the whole thing. We can't slow down. We can't have guardrails. We have to beat China." There's also been this undercurrent of figuring out how you cooperate, how you're still making money without stifling innovation. This has played out into disputes within Trump's own cabinet. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent versus Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. I have loved the drama of it all.
Sophie Kleeman: The girls are fighting.

Leah Feiger: The girls are fighting. But frankly, for as much as Bessent spent the last week throwing Lutnick entirely under the rug, it kind of turns out, and Hugo found, that Trump has been really playing that middle and siding with Lutnick in a lot of this. So this new rule is going to be really interesting. I'm very curious about it getting enforced. I'm curious about how it's going to also be talked about and communicated this week on the ground actually in China. Hugo's newsletter that published Wednesday night gets into this, and basically what officials have told him quietly is that there probably isn't going to be a lot of movement on AI as Trump arrives, really because of the Nvidia scandal, because there has been so much consternation of quote, unquote Chinese spies everywhere. And this conversation is a little bit at a standstill. So new rule, conversations happening, maybe no results. I don't know. Is that politics as usual? Perhaps.

Brian Barrett: I have a couple questions. One, this is a dumb one, I'm sorry, but we just heard Donald Trump saying, when asked about outages, that if you're big, then people will go for you, even though that has nothing to do with what's going on. So my question, Leah, the eternal question with Donald Trump, how much do we think he actually knows or cares about any of this versus whoever was in the room with him last has told him a thing that sounds good?

Leah Feiger: Oh, I think that's a huge part of it. Ultimately, and I should have this tattooed on my forehead, which is that similar rules to these already existed. They existed in the Biden era. Trump rolled them back in 2025. Again, unclear how much of that context is memorable to the administration or to Trump himself. But I think the underlying current, really for him, for as far as we've been able to understand from his public statements and his private ones that people have been able to report out, is that he wants the US to be competitive. Fist on table, be competitive. Whether that means we're selling chips or not selling chips, they're not very complicated thoughts. I'm sorry to say. I don't know how else to put it other than I'm not sure that the minutia is that interesting to him. And frankly, the minutia is barely interesting to the rest of us.
Sophie Kleeman: It's deeply unsexy. It's deeply unsexy.

Leah Feiger: It's like every time that we're writing an article on this, and I'm sure that you struggle with this as well, Sophie, I'm like, "And here's our context paragraph where I spell out exactly what Megaspeed meant for chips."
Sophie Kleeman: It reads like a white paper. Yeah.
Leah Feiger: It's horrible. Whereas it's much easier to say, "No, we must be competitive with China. Also, we have to work with China." OK, what does that mean when you're spelling it out?
Sophie Kleeman: I mean, my question too, not to put on my conspiracy theory hat again, but I think-
Brian Barrett: Dit it.
Leah Feiger: This is when we unveil you as our ... This is why you're here.
Sophie Kleeman: Resident conspiracy theorist. I mean, so the reporting about this, it was a little bit hedged. It was like they are moving toward closing a loophole.

Sophie Kleeman: So my question is, are they just trying to get out ahead of, they were caught with their pants down in some respects with the Nvidia, the Megaspeed, all that stuff. And so now they're like, "OK, we need to sort of look like we're doing something. So we're just going to say that we're going to do this, and maybe we will or maybe we won't, but we're just going to be like, OK, look, look over here instead of over there."

Leah Feiger: I mean, 100 percent. Back in September, that's when we were told that this Cold War era-style hotline was going to be coming between China and the US, that this was going to be how we were going to address these issues. There was going to be an open dialogue. And look, that's still apparently, Hugo is learning, is still being discussed, is still on the table, but also to me just reads as to exactly what you're saying, which is here's an option, here's another option. I'm not defending anyone here, to be entirely clear, but there is a thin line. I mean, the US and Trump has gone for China hard with trade restrictions. China has not liked that. They've responded with restrictions of their own, rare earth exports et al. So there is this line that they have to draw of, yes, we are anti-China. They have to appease the anti-China hawks in the party while also having to work with the richest nation around. And so it's a very tricky balance.

Brian Barrett: One last politics thing to mention, just because it's significant. It has nothing to do with export controls. On Wednesday, the incoming head of the House Oversight Committee directed Donald Trump Jr. son of Donald Trump, to preserve all records related to his lavish wedding celebrations and his many business ventures. That's not the only records preservation, "Hey, we're going to investigate you" stuff going on this week. We had representative Robert Garcia, incoming head of the House Oversight Committee issuing a similar record preservation request to Eric Trump along with Donald Trump Jr. related to their wildly controversial crypto firm, World Liberty Financial, along with brother-in-law, Jared Kushner, who runs a Saudi backed investment firm while also serving as a presidential envoy to the Middle East. Leah, not a question so much as a statement, but sparks are flying. Or they're about to.
Leah Feiger: Sparks are flying.
Brian Barrett: Not the romantic kind, sorry. I mean more excitement and investigations coming.

Leah Feiger: Look, within hours of Democrats winning the midterms, they immediately started saying that investigations were coming. You're going to be seeing evidence of this really soon. The fact that the Trump family is going to be at the core of this already is expected, but they're coming in hard. Also listed in these record preservation requests was Stephen Miller, now White House chief of staff, for all of his activities regarding ICE invasions of American cities over this past year. We have Susie Wiles, the ex-chief of staff. We have Kristi Noem, we have Corey Lewandowski, former DHS officials. There's a lot here that [Robert] Garcia and the oversight committee are going to be digging into. And regardless of when all of these things kind of begin, at the very least, this is our first official indication that things are coming. They're going to drag people in front of Congress. I can't wait to see this play out. This is going to be huge. They're going for everyone. Everyone in the Trump orbit is going to be called in here.
Brian Barrett: Coming up after the break, we're going to share our WIRED/TIRED picks for the week. Stay with us.
Leah Feiger: It is time for our WIRED and TIRED segment. As usual, whatever is new and cool is WIRED and whatever passé thing we're over is TIRED. Brian, can you go first?

Brian Barrett: I'd love to go first. It would be an honor. My WIRED. So this episode is coming out on the same day that Grand Theft Auto 6 comes out, the most highly anticipated sequel for video games maybe ever.
Sophie Kleeman: Oh my god, Brian, are you a gamer?
Brian Barrett: No, I'm not. I'm not. But my WIRED is go ahead and take the day off of work. I support that. I think taking the day off of work—
Sophie Kleeman: I'm holding you to that. Absolutely.

Brian Barrett: ... to play Grand Theft Auto 6 is totally fine and normal. I'm supportive of this. Again, I don't have a console that can play it. I have a Switch in my house that nobody plays, but I recognize that it's a big cultural moment. So go ahead. Don't feel bad about it. And I'll do the same for March Madness when that comes around. So that's my WIRED. You've got my permission, America, to do that.
Sophie Kleeman: Thank you so much.

Brian Barrett: And my TIRED? I do just want to point out, Sophie brought this up earlier. I think the only people who say we got this multiple times in a couple of days are people who don't got it. I think if you've got it, you don't need to say that you've got it. So saying you've got it is TIRED because it really suggests to me that you probably don't got it.
Leah Feiger: Very sad. All right. Sophie, what do you think?
Sophie Kleeman: OK. I have two. Is that allowed? Am I allowed to have two?
Leah Feiger: Two WIREDs and two TIREDs?
Sophie Kleeman: I sure do. I'm an overachiever.
Brian Barrett: Two of each? Wow.

Sophie Kleeman: WIRED is a jacket that I've seen all the fashion girlies on my Twitter feed talking about, which is a silk and fur trend.

Sophie Kleeman: OK. So that's my WIRED. My second WIRED and TIRED. TIRED, Chonkers, the sea lion. WIRED, Neil the seal.

Leah Feiger: No further explanation needed. Yeah. Google it, people. OK. My WIRED and TIRED is, I'm very saddened, which I guess is my TIRED, by everyone is doing their Black Friday sales right now and very early. news.title: Intuit to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion
news.title_en: Intuit to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion
news.author: Jordan Novet
news.content_snippet:
